title: Take On Me
description: The pencil-sketch romance that made rotoscoping famous — restored in 4K.

pops.text: Started life as an instrumental called "The Juicy Fruit Song," written by Magne Furuholmen and Pål Waaktaar-Savoy in their earlier rock band Bridges — years before Morten Harket joined.
Released three times before anyone cared: the 1984 version flopped in the UK, the 1985 re-record flopped too — until the new video changed everything.
The pencil-sketch look is rotoscoping: live footage traced frame by frame. Animators hand-drew about 3,000 frames — 16 weeks of animation work.
Directed by Steve Barron — the same man behind Michael Jackson's "Billie Jean" — who won Best Direction for this at the 1986 MTV VMAs.
Harket's vocal spans two and a half octaves, soaring to falsetto at the end of the chorus — called one of the hardest-to-sing choruses in pop.
The two villains were played by Philip Jackson (later Inspector Japp in Poirot) and Alfie Curtis (Dr. Evazan in Star Wars).
The girl in the video was Bunty Bailey, Harket's real-life girlfriend at the time — the comic-book romance was basically a true love story.
Hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 on October 19, 1985 — the first Norwegian group ever to top the US chart.
In the UK it sat at No. 2 for three weeks, blocked by Jennifer Rush's "The Power of Love" — that year's biggest UK single.
In September 2024 it became the first 1980s music video to reach 2 billion YouTube views — 40 years after it was recorded.

title: Thriller
description: A date-night movie becomes a werewolf nightmare — the most imitated music video ever made.

pops.text: Songwriter Rod Temperton's first demo was called "Starlight." He brainstormed hundreds of titles — "Midnight Man" among them — until he woke up with "Thriller" stuck in his head.
Horror legend Vincent Price recorded his closing narration in just two takes. Temperton wrote Price's script in the back of a taxi on the way to the studio.
Michael hired director John Landis after seeing An American Werewolf in London — he specifically wanted transformation scenes like Landis's.
Shot on 35mm film with feature-film production values — Landis wanted a theatrical short that would bring short films back to cinemas.
Final cost was about $500,000 — roughly ten times the average early-'80s video budget. They paid for it by selling a behind-the-scenes documentary to MTV and Showtime.
The iconic red jacket was designed by Deborah Nadoolman Landis — the director's wife and a professional costume designer.
The zombie dance was choreographed by Michael Peters together with Michael himself — now one of the most copied routines in history, recreated every Halloween.
Co-star Ola Ray was a former Playboy Playmate, spotted for the role through her modeling work.
MTV debuted it December 2, 1983, running it 3–5 times a day. Ratings ran about ten times the network's normal audience — and album sales spiked to a million copies a week.
In 2009 "Thriller" became the first music video ever preserved in the Library of Congress National Film Registry.

title: Girls Just Want to Have Fun
description: Cyndi sneaks out past her grumpy dad and dances through Manhattan's Lower East Side.

pops.text: Not Lauper's creation — Philadelphia musician Robert Hazard wrote and demoed it in 1979 from a man's point of view. Lauper refused to sing it as written and reworked it into a girl-power anthem.
Lauper was so unsure of the track she cut demo after demo in different styles — nothing clicked until she leaned into a bouncy, summer-vacation-commercial sound.
Her very first solo single, released September 6, 1983 — the breakout that made a former bar-band singer a global star overnight.
Shot on the Lower East Side in summer 1983 on a shoestring — under $35,000, volunteer cast, borrowed gear. MTV put it in heavy rotation back when the channel played videos around the clock.
Dad casting was perfect '80s weirdness: wrestling legend "Captain" Lou Albano plays her disapproving father, and her real-life mother plays mom. Her attorney, manager, brother, and dog also appear.

Lauper deliberately cast women of every background dancing together so every little girl watching could see herself on screen. Decades later, protesters carried signs reading "Girls Just Want to Have Fun-damental Rights."
Peaked at #2 on the Billboard Hot 100 in March 1984 — blocked by Van Halen's "Jump." Still spent 25 straight weeks on the chart.
Made history at the first-ever MTV VMAs in 1984, winning the first Best Female Video award — and nominated for Video of the Year the same night.
Earned two Grammy nominations, and that night she won Best New Artist while the album took Best Album Package.
Parent album She's So Unusual was the first debut by a female artist to land four top-five Hot 100 hits. The video crossed one billion YouTube views in January 2022.

title: Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go
description: Bubblegum pop at London's Brixton Academy in the iconic CHOOSE LIFE shirts.

pops.text: The title came from a sleepy note Andrew Ridgeley scribbled for his parents — he meant "wake me up before you go" but doubled "up," then doubled "go" to cover the mistake. He still keeps the original note.
George Michael wrote, produced, and arranged the whole track himself in two days. He claims a single take with no overdubs — and the drum machine stayed in because the real drummer was late.
Released in the UK on May 14, 1984, it debuted at #4 and hit #1 seven days later — Wham!'s first UK chart-topper.
Repeated the trick in the US: three weeks at #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in November 1984 — their first American #1.
Directed by Andy Morahan and filmed at Brixton Academy in South London, the duo playing to mostly teenage extras.
The "CHOOSE LIFE" shirts were Katharine Hamnett's bold anti-war, anti-drug design — they kicked off a massive '80s fashion craze.
Blink and you'll miss it: the video ends with a cheesy on-screen ad — "GO-GO BUY IT! thank you" — on the final black frame.
George Michael was never that fond of it — he called it "undoubtedly the most remembered Wham! song because it is that much more stupid than anything else."
VH1 ranked it #28 on its "100 Greatest Songs of the '80s."
In Zoolander it soundtracks the gasoline fight scene — but only as a temp placeholder. Sum 41, hired to write an original song, saw the rough cut and insisted the Wham! track stay.

title: Try Everything
description: Shakira in the studio, intercut with scenes from Disney's Zootopia.

pops.text: Shakira's first-ever animated-film voice role: she plays Gazelle, Zootopia's pop superstar, who performs this song at the movie's climactic concert.
The video is half studio session, half movie magic — Shakira in headphones belting into a mic, cutting back and forth with Zootopia clips.
Sia co-wrote it with Norwegian hitmakers Stargate — and years before Shakira, girl group Fifth Harmony cut a version in 2013 that never got released.
Shakira's first single released under Walt Disney Records, kicking off the Zootopia soundtrack on January 26, 2016.
Earned a 2017 Grammy nomination for Best Song Written for Visual Media — the category for songs made for movies and TV.
Debuted on the Billboard Hot 100 at No. 63 after the video dropped — 33,000 downloads and about 3 million US streams in its first tracking week.
A genuine global hit: No. 1 in Lebanon and Japan's international chart, and 4× platinum in the US.
The movie was no slouch: Zootopia crossed $1 billion worldwide in June 2016 — only the fourth animated film ever to do so.
Kids worldwide got their own version: re-recorded in Mandarin, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, Polish, and Ukrainian so Gazelle could sing in each country's dub.
Billboard named it one of the 12 best Disney songs of the 21st century in 2020, and it later landed at No. 19 on their all-time greatest Disney songs chart.

title: Margaritaville
description: The official audio upload of Jimmy's biggest hit — the song that built an empire.

pops.text: Buffett started writing it in Austin, Texas, right after a burrito and his first-ever margarita — finishing the lyrics that same night on a friend's deck, then polishing it in Key West.
His working title wasn't "Margaritaville" — he first wanted "Wasting Away in Austin, Texasville," then decided the cocktail deserved the headline.

When Buffett told producer Norbert Putnam he wanted to write about losing his flip-flop and salt shaker, Putnam said: "That's a terrible idea for a song." Days later Buffett returned with the finished tune.
Putnam had produced Elvis, but Buffett made him leave Nashville for a Miami studio — reasoning: if you're singing about beach life, you record near the water.
Buffett's biggest solo hit ever: #8 on the Billboard Hot 100, #1 Easy Listening. Billboard ranked it the 14th biggest pop single of all 1977.
The "lost shaker of salt" line was literal — the idea started after a Key West night where he lost a flip-flop, stepped on a pop-top can tab, and couldn't find the salt for his margarita.
In July 1977 it sat in the Top 10 alongside Streisand, Manilow, and Frampton — and it's the only one from that week's Top 10 now in both the Grammy Hall of Fame and the National Recording Registry.
Buffett was thrilled it was a hit because it finally let him buy his own boat. It grew into an empire: restaurants, resorts, a Broadway musical, a SiriusXM channel, his own blenders.
In 2023 the song entered the Library of Congress National Recording Registry for cultural importance.
After Buffett's passing on September 1, 2023, it stormed back onto the Hot 100 at #38 — its first appearance in 46 years.

title: Bohemian Rhapsody
description: The diamond formation of glowing faces — the official HD remaster.

pops.text: Freddie Mercury wrote the whole thing — a "mock opera" stitched from three separate songs he'd written, fully mapped out in his head before the band hit the studio.
At nearly six minutes, label EMI said it was far too long for radio and pushed to cut it. Mercury refused — then DJ Kenny Everett played his "never play this" tape 14 times in one weekend.
Recording took three weeks across five studios. With only 24-track tape, layers were "bounced down" so many times the final mix sat on eighth-generation tape.
The opera section alone needed about 180 vocal overdubs — Mercury, Brian May, and Roger Taylor sang 10–12 hours a day until the harmonies stacked into a giant fake choir.
The most expensive single ever made at the time — all that studio-hopping and hundreds of overdubs nearly bankrupted the band.

The video was shot in under four hours at Elstree Studios for about £4,500 — because the band was touring and couldn't mime it on Top of the Pops. The diamond face pose recreates the Queen II album cover.
Chart monster: nine weeks at UK #1 in 1975, then #1 again for five weeks after Mercury's death in 1991 — the first song to top the UK charts twice with the same recording.
After the 2018 biopic it became the most-streamed song of the 20th century; in 2022 the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry.
A 2023 auction of Mercury's belongings revealed his handwritten draft — first titled "Mongolian Rhapsody," with "Mongolian" crossed out and "Bohemian" written in.
Rolling Stone ranked it #17 on its 2021 "500 Greatest Songs"; readers voted Mercury's vocal the greatest in rock history; it entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2004.

title: Billie Jean
description: A paparazzo chases Michael through a city where the sidewalk lights up under his feet.

pops.text: Quincy Jones didn't want it on Thriller — he disliked the intro and the bassline, but Michael fought for both, calling the bassline "the jelly" that makes you want to dance.
Jones also wanted to retitle it "Not My Lover," worried buyers would think it was about tennis star Billie Jean King. Michael refused to budge.
Engineer Bruce Swedien mixed it 91 times — then they went back and picked mix #2. Michael sang the lead vocal in a single take, through a six-foot cardboard tube.
The famous bassline was played by Louis Johnson of the Brothers Johnson, who tried nearly every bass he owned before settling on a Yamaha.
The light-up sidewalk tiles were director Steve Barron's "Midas touch" concept — everything Michael touches glows. Barron got the gig after Michael saw his Human League clip.
Same Steve Barron who later directed a-ha's "Take On Me" — winning Best Direction at the 1986 VMAs for it.
The video broke MTV's color barrier — the first by a Black artist in heavy rotation, after CBS chief Walter Yetnikoff threatened to pull all CBS videos if MTV kept refusing it.
Seven weeks at #1 on the Hot 100, No. 1 in 10 countries, and the second-biggest-selling US single of 1983.
Months later, this is the song Michael debuted the moonwalk to — on the Motown 25 TV special in May 1983.
Daryl Hall has said Michael told him directly he "copped" the groove from Hall & Oates' "I Can't Go for That (No Can Do)."

title: Like a Prayer
description: A dream of a saint come to life amid burning crosses — the video that cost her a Pepsi deal.

pops.text: Co-written and co-produced with Patrick Leonard — Madonna reportedly nailed her vocals in a single take, demo vocal straight to the record.
Listen for the guitar before the door slam — that's Prince, uncredited. He recorded his parts in Minneapolis and mailed the tapes under an alias to dodge bootleggers.
The gospel punch comes from the Andraé Crouch Choir lifting the choruses into something church-sized.
Her seventh US No. 1 — three weeks atop the Hot 100, and No. 1 in the UK, Canada, Australia, Italy, and more.
Directed by Mary Lambert, who wanted to explore the link between sexual and religious ecstasy — and to take the Klan's burning cross and "turn that on its head."
The Vatican condemned it and the Pope urged a boycott in Italy; religious and family groups protested its broadcast.
Pepsi had just signed her to a $5 million endorsement deal — then killed it over the video. She kept the money anyway.
The dream-kiss with the Black saint was loosely inspired by Saint Martin de Porres, patron saint of racial harmony.
In 2023 Madonna publicly thanked Pepsi on the VMAs stage for airing the original commercial — 34 years after they pulled it.
It found a whole new audience in 2024's Deadpool & Wolverine, soundtracking the finale and sending the song back up the charts.

title: Livin' on a Prayer
description: Black-and-white rehearsal explodes into a color arena show, Jon flying over the crowd.

pops.text: Jon Bon Jovi didn't like it at first — he thought the piano-written demo was too soft for a guitar band. Desmond Child and Richie Sambora got on their hands and knees and begged him to record it.
The first draft's hook was "We've gotta hold on" — Child told Jon "that's just the B section, let's write the chorus now," and the "Whoa, we're halfway there" chorus was born.
Tommy and Gina were almost Johnny and Gina — Jon vetoed "Johnny" because everyone would think he was singing about himself.
The names came from Child's real-life friends, a high-school couple who'd fallen on hard times.
That talking-guitar intro is Richie Sambora on a talk box — the guitar signal runs through a tube into his mouth so he shapes the sound with his lips.
The video bursts from black-and-white into color as Jon, strapped into a harness, flies over the arena crowd on overhead wires.
Filmed September 17, 1986, at the Grand Olympic Auditorium in Los Angeles, directed by Wayne Isham.
Four weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100 — making Bon Jovi the first hard rock band ever with consecutive No. 1 singles.
VH1's voters named it the No. 1 Greatest Song of the '80s in 2006.
The video crossed 1 billion YouTube views in January 2023 — decades after its release.

title: Total Eclipse of the Heart
description: A gothic fever dream in a boys' boarding school — doves, fencing, ninjas.

pops.text: It started as "Vampires in Love" — Jim Steinman wrote it for a Nosferatu musical, and he says the lyrics are "really like vampire lines... all about the darkness."
The "Turn around, bright eyes" hook dates back even further — to Steinman's 1969 college musical.
Meat Loaf wanted it for himself and was furious when it went to Tyler instead — both camps have told that story differently for 40 years.
The soaring "turn around" counter-vocals aren't Tyler — that's Steinman regular Rory Dodd, who sang the demo when Steinman first played it for her at the piano.
The band is secretly the E Street Band's rhythm section — Roy Bittan and Max Weinberg, plus Rick Derringer on guitar.
Directed by Russell Mulcahy — the man who directed the very first video ever played on MTV ("Video Killed the Radio Star") and later the movie Highlander.
Filmed at England's Holloway Sanatorium, a former Victorian asylum — fitting for a video Tyler herself tweeted she still can't explain, 39 years later.
For years fans swore one of the glowing-eyed schoolboys was Italian footballer Gianfranco Zola. He denied it in 2012.
No. 1 in the US, UK, and Australia — making Tyler the first and only Welsh artist ever to top the Hot 100.
During the 2017 total solar eclipse she performed it on a cruise ship with DNCE as the eclipse hit totality — sales jumped 500% that week.

title: Born in the U.S.A.
description: Live E Street firepower intercut with images of veterans and small-town America.

pops.text: It's a protest song about mistreated Vietnam veterans — Springsteen calls it his "soldiers story." The working title was just "Vietnam."
The first version was a bleak acoustic demo cut in January 1982 for the Nebraska sessions — the roaring band version came later.
Ronald Reagan name-checked Springsteen at a 1984 New Jersey campaign stop. Days later in Pittsburgh, Bruce deadpanned: "I don't think he's been listening to this one."
Reagan wasn't the last — Dole, Buchanan, and Trump all tried to claim it; Springsteen publicly rebuked every one of them.
The title idea came from filmmaker Paul Schrader, who sent Bruce a script called Born in the U.S.A. about a struggling rock band. Bruce gave him "Light of Day" for the film instead.
The video was directed by filmmaker John Sayles, mixing concert footage with images of soldiers, graveyards, and kids.
The album spun off seven Top 10 singles — tying the all-time record shared with Michael Jackson's Thriller.
It was the best-selling album of 1985, spent seven weeks at No. 1, and has sold over 30 million copies worldwide.
The cover — Bruce's backside against a giant flag — was shot by Annie Leibovitz and helped turn "Bossmania" into a full-blown phenomenon.
It was the first CD ever manufactured in America — pressed at CBS/Sony's new Terre Haute, Indiana plant in September 1984.
